title: 8. Key Papers and Reading List
intro: An annotated reading list for building computational cortical columns, organised by theme: the biology of the column, neuron and synapse models, plasticity and sparse codes, HTM, the Thousand Brains Theory and Monty, other column models, simulators and neuromorphic hardware, and books. Items marked 'Start here' form a short core path.

blocks.text: Entries are grouped by theme and roughly ordered within each theme from most foundational to most specialised. Items marked 'Start here' form a short core path: read those first, in this suggested order — Mountcastle 1997, Harris & Shepherd 2015, Gerstner et al. 2014 (chapters 1, 5 and 19), Brunel 2000, Song, Miller & Abbott 2000, Diehl & Cook 2015, Hawkins & Ahmad 2016, Hawkins, Ahmad & Cui 2017, Hawkins 2021, Potjans & Diesmann 2014, then Rao & Ballard 1999. That is about two to three weeks of focused reading and gives you the shared vocabulary of the whole topic. Everything else is for when a specific question comes up while building.

items: Start here: Mountcastle, V. B. (1997). The columnar organization of the neocortex. Brain. — The definitive statement of the column and minicolumn as repeated units; the hypothesis Hawkins builds on.

Mountcastle, V. B. (1957). Modality and topographic properties of single neurons of cat's somatic sensory cortex. Journal of Neurophysiology. — The original discovery of vertical columns of cells sharing modality and receptive-field location.

Hubel, D. H. & Wiesel, T. N. (1962). Receptive fields, binocular interaction and functional architecture in the cat's visual cortex. Journal of Physiology. — Simple and complex cells and orientation columns; the vocabulary of visual cortex.

Mountcastle, V. B. (1978). An organizing principle for cerebral function: the unit module and the distributed system. In Edelman, G. M. & Mountcastle, V. B., The Mindful Brain. MIT Press. — The essay proposing one common cortical algorithm across areas.

Hubel, D. H. & Wiesel, T. N. (1977). Ferrier lecture: functional architecture of macaque monkey visual cortex. Proceedings of the Royal Society B. — Ocular dominance and orientation hypercolumns in primate V1.

Lorente de Nó, R. (1938). Architectonics and structure of the cerebral cortex. In Fulton, J. F., Physiology of the Nervous System. Oxford University Press. — The early proposal of vertical chains of neurons as the elementary cortical unit.

Start here: Harris, K. D. & Shepherd, G. M. G. (2015). The neocortical circuit: themes and variations. Nature Neuroscience. — The best modern summary of layer-by-layer circuitry, including where the canonical picture fails.

Horton, J. C. & Adams, D. L. (2005). The cortical column: a structure without a function. Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society B. — The essential sceptical counterpoint; read it before claiming columns are computational units.
Buxhoeveden, D. P. & Casanova, M. F. (2002). The minicolumn hypothesis in neuroscience. Brain. — Review of minicolumn anatomy, sizes and evidence.
Douglas, R. J. & Martin, K. A. C. (2004). Neuronal circuits of the neocortex. Annual Review of Neuroscience. — Canonical circuit, recurrent amplification and quantitative wiring in one review.
Thomson, A. M. & Lamy, C. (2007). Functional maps of neocortical local circuitry. Frontiers in Neuroscience. — Paired-recording connectivity between layers and cell types, with numbers.

Sherman, S. M. & Guillery, R. W. (1998). On the actions that one nerve cell can have on another: distinguishing 'drivers' from 'modulators'. PNAS. — The driver/modulator distinction that underlies thalamocortical models.

Markram, H., Toledo-Rodriguez, M., Wang, Y., Gupta, A., Silberberg, G. & Wu, C. (2004). Interneurons of the neocortical inhibitory system. Nature Reviews Neuroscience. — Classic taxonomy of interneuron morphology and firing types.
Tremblay, R., Lee, S. & Rudy, B. (2016). GABAergic interneurons in the neocortex: from cellular properties to circuits. Neuron. — The modern PV/SST/VIP-based view of inhibition.

Hodgkin, A. L. & Huxley, A. F. (1952). A quantitative description of membrane current and its application to conduction and excitation in nerve. Journal of Physiology. — The conductance-based model all detailed neurons descend from.

Lapicque, L. (1907). Recherches quantitatives sur l'excitation électrique des nerfs traitée comme une polarisation. Journal de Physiologie et de Pathologie Générale. — The historical origin of the integrate-and-fire idea.
Izhikevich, E. M. (2003). Simple model of spiking neurons. IEEE Transactions on Neural Networks. — Two equations, four parameters, most cortical firing patterns; ideal for hardware.
Izhikevich, E. M. (2004). Which model to use for cortical spiking neurons? IEEE Transactions on Neural Networks. — A cost/features comparison table of neuron models.

Brette, R. & Gerstner, W. (2005). Adaptive exponential integrate-and-fire model as an effective description of neuronal activity. Journal of Neurophysiology. — AdEx, the best accuracy-per-cost point-neuron model.

Start here: Brunel, N. (2000). Dynamics of sparsely connected networks of excitatory and inhibitory spiking neurons. Journal of Computational Neuroscience. — The phase diagram of E/I LIF networks; explains why your network is silent, synchronous or irregular.

van Vreeswijk, C. & Sompolinsky, H. (1996). Chaos in neuronal networks with balanced excitatory and inhibitory activity. Science. — Why balanced excitation and inhibition give irregular cortical firing.

Tsodyks, M. V. & Markram, H. (1997). The neural code between neocortical pyramidal neurons depends on neurotransmitter release probability. PNAS. — Short-term depression and the standard synapse model used in detailed and point-neuron models.
Schiller, J., Major, G., Koester, H. J. & Schiller, Y. (2000). NMDA spikes in basal dendrites of cortical pyramidal neurons. Nature. — The dendritic event HTM's distal segments abstract.
Poirazi, P., Brannon, T. & Mel, B. W. (2003). Pyramidal neuron as two-layer neural network. Neuron. — Dendritic branches as nonlinear subunits.

Polsky, A., Mel, B. W. & Schiller, J. (2004). Computational subunits in thin dendrites of pyramidal cells. Nature Neuroscience. — Experimental evidence that branches integrate locally and nonlinearly.

Larkum, M. (2013). A cellular mechanism for cortical associations: an organizing principle for the cerebral cortex. Trends in Neurosciences. — Apical-tuft coupling of feedforward and feedback input; key for layered column models.

Major, G., Larkum, M. E. & Schiller, J. (2013). Active properties of neocortical pyramidal neuron dendrites. Annual Review of Neuroscience. — Comprehensive review of dendritic spikes and their computational roles.
Hebb, D. O. (1949). The Organization of Behavior. Wiley. — The source of the cell-assembly and Hebbian learning ideas.
Oja, E. (1982). A simplified neuron model as a principal component analyzer. Journal of Mathematical Biology. — Normalised Hebbian learning; the simplest stable rule.

Bienenstock, E. L., Cooper, L. N. & Munro, P. W. (1982). Theory for the development of neuron selectivity: orientation specificity and binocular interaction in visual cortex. Journal of Neuroscience. — BCM: a sliding threshold that makes Hebbian learning selective and stable.

Markram, H., Lübke, J., Frotscher, M. & Sakmann, B. (1997). Regulation of synaptic efficacy by coincidence of postsynaptic APs and EPSPs. Science. — Early demonstration of spike-timing dependence in neocortex.

Bi, G. & Poo, M. (1998). Synaptic modifications in cultured hippocampal neurons: dependence on spike timing, synaptic strength, and postsynaptic cell type. Journal of Neuroscience. — The classic STDP window measurement.

Start here: Song, S., Miller, K. D. & Abbott, L. F. (2000). Competitive Hebbian learning through spike-timing-dependent synaptic plasticity. Nature Neuroscience. — Pair-based STDP as a model rule and its competitive consequences.

van Rossum, M. C. W., Bi, G. Q. & Turrigiano, G. G. (2000). Stable Hebbian learning from spike timing-dependent plasticity. Journal of Neuroscience. — Weight-dependent (multiplicative) STDP and unimodal weight distributions.
Pfister, J.-P. & Gerstner, W. (2006). Triplets of spikes in a model of spike timing-dependent plasticity. Journal of Neuroscience. — The triplet rule that fixes pair-STDP's frequency dependence.

Turrigiano, G. G., Leslie, K. R., Desai, N. S., Rutherford, L. C. & Nelson, S. B. (1998). Activity-dependent scaling of quantal amplitude in neocortical neurons. Nature. — Synaptic scaling, the main homeostatic mechanism used in models.
Turrigiano, G. G. (2008). The self-tuning neuron: synaptic scaling of excitatory synapses. Cell. — Review of homeostatic plasticity.

Vogels, T. P., Sprekeler, H., Zenke, F., Clopath, C. & Gerstner, W. (2011). Inhibitory plasticity balances excitation and inhibition in sensory pathways and memory networks. Science. — A simple inhibitory STDP rule that self-tunes E/I balance.

Masquelier, T. & Thorpe, S. J. (2007). Unsupervised learning of visual features through spike timing dependent plasticity. PLoS Computational Biology. — STDP plus first-spike competition learns features.

Start here: Diehl, P. U. & Cook, M. (2015). Unsupervised learning of digit recognition using spike-timing-dependent plasticity. Frontiers in Computational Neuroscience. — The STDP + lateral inhibition + adaptive threshold recipe; a baseline for any learning column.
Thorpe, S., Delorme, A. & Van Rullen, R. (2001). Spike-based strategies for rapid processing. Neural Networks. — Rank-order and latency codes.
Olshausen, B. A. & Field, D. J. (1996). Emergence of simple-cell receptive field properties by learning a sparse code for natural images. Nature. — Sparse coding reproduces V1 receptive fields.
Olshausen, B. A. & Field, D. J. (2004). Sparse coding of sensory inputs. Current Opinion in Neurobiology. — Short review of why cortex might use sparse codes.
Kanerva, P. (1988). Sparse Distributed Memory. MIT Press. — The high-dimensional sparse memory model that anticipates SDRs.

Start here: Hawkins, J. & Ahmad, S. (2016). Why neurons have thousands of synapses, a theory of sequence memory in neocortex. Frontiers in Neural Circuits. — The HTM neuron and temporal memory, with biological justification.
Ahmad, S. & Hawkins, J. (2015). Properties of sparse distributed representations and their application to hierarchical temporal memory. arXiv. — Capacity and noise robustness of SDRs.

Ahmad, S. & Hawkins, J. (2016). How do neurons operate on sparse distributed representations? A mathematical theory of sparsity, neurons and active dendrites. arXiv. — The false-match formulas behind dendritic segment design.

Cui, Y., Ahmad, S. & Hawkins, J. (2016). Continuous online sequence learning with an unsupervised neural network model. Neural Computation. — Temporal memory benchmarked against LSTM and other sequence learners.

Cui, Y., Ahmad, S. & Hawkins, J. (2017). The HTM spatial pooler — a neocortical algorithm for online sparse distributed coding. Frontiers in Computational Neuroscience. — The spatial pooler specified and evaluated.
Purdy, S. (2016). Encoding data for HTM systems. arXiv. — How to design encoders that produce good SDRs.
Lavin, A. & Ahmad, S. (2015). Evaluating real-time anomaly detection algorithms – the Numenta Anomaly Benchmark. IEEE ICMLA. — The NAB benchmark for streaming anomaly detection.
Ahmad, S., Lavin, A., Purdy, S. & Agha, Z. (2017). Unsupervised real-time anomaly detection for streaming data. Neurocomputing. — HTM anomaly detection in practice.
Hawkins, J. & Blakeslee, S. (2004). On Intelligence. Times Books. — The popular account of the memory-prediction framework that led to HTM.

Start here: Hawkins, J., Ahmad, S. & Cui, Y. (2017). A theory of how columns in the neocortex enable learning the structure of the world. Frontiers in Neural Circuits. — Columns learn objects as features at locations and vote; the first Thousand Brains paper.

Lewis, M., Purdy, S., Ahmad, S. & Hawkins, J. (2019). Locations in the neocortex: a theory of sensorimotor object recognition using cortical grid cells. Frontiers in Neural Circuits. — Grid-cell-like location codes inside columns.

Hawkins, J., Lewis, M., Klukas, M., Purdy, S. & Ahmad, S. (2019). A framework for intelligence and cortical function based on grid cells in the neocortex. Frontiers in Neural Circuits. — The full framework: reference frames, displacement cells, voting.
Start here: Hawkins, J. (2021). A Thousand Brains: A New Theory of Intelligence. Basic Books. — The accessible overview that motivates this whole topic.

Clay, V., Leadholm, N. & Hawkins, J. (2024). The Thousand Brains Project: a new paradigm for sensorimotor intelligence. arXiv. — Design of Monty, its learning modules and the Cortical Messaging Protocol (check the arXiv page for the full author list).
O'Keefe, J. & Dostrovsky, J. (1971). The hippocampus as a spatial map. Preliminary evidence from unit activity in the freely-moving rat. Brain Research. — The discovery of place cells.
Hafting, T., Fyhn, M., Molden, S., Moser, M.-B. & Moser, E. I. (2005). Microstructure of a spatial map in the entorhinal cortex. Nature. — The discovery of grid cells.

Moser, E. I., Kropff, E. & Moser, M.-B. (2008). Place cells, grid cells, and the brain's spatial representation system. Annual Review of Neuroscience. — Review of the spatial system Thousand Brains borrows from.
Constantinescu, A. O., O'Reilly, J. X. & Behrens, T. E. J. (2016). Organizing conceptual knowledge in humans with a gridlike code. Science. — Evidence for grid-like codes beyond physical space.
Douglas, R. J., Martin, K. A. C. & Whitteridge, D. (1989). A canonical microcircuit for neocortex. Neural Computation. — The original canonical microcircuit.
Douglas, R. J. & Martin, K. A. C. (1991). A functional microcircuit for cat visual cortex. Journal of Physiology. — The full experimental and modelling account.

Binzegger, T., Douglas, R. J. & Martin, K. A. C. (2004). A quantitative map of the circuit of cat primary visual cortex. Journal of Neuroscience. — Synapse counts between cell types and layers; source of many model connection tables.

Start here: Potjans, T. C. & Diesmann, M. (2014). The cell-type specific cortical microcircuit: relating structure and activity in a full-scale spiking network model. Cerebral Cortex. — The standard full-density spiking microcircuit and benchmark.

Start here: Rao, R. P. N. & Ballard, D. H. (1999). Predictive coding in the visual cortex: a functional interpretation of some extra-classical receptive-field effects. Nature Neuroscience. — The reference predictive-coding model.
Friston, K. (2010). The free-energy principle: a unified brain theory? Nature Reviews Neuroscience. — The general framework predictive coding sits inside.
Bastos, A. M., Usrey, W. M., Adams, R. A., Mangun, G. R., Fries, P. & Friston, K. J. (2012). Canonical microcircuits for predictive coding. Neuron. — The laminar mapping of predictions and errors.
Keller, G. B. & Mrsic-Flogel, T. D. (2018). Predictive processing: a canonical cortical computation. Neuron. — Mismatch responses and a circuit-level predictive-processing proposal.
Markram, H. et al. (2015). Reconstruction and simulation of neocortical microcircuitry. Cell. — The Blue Brain digital reconstruction.

Billeh, Y. N. et al. (2020). Systematic integration of structural and functional data into multi-scale models of mouse primary visual cortex. Neuron. — The Allen V1 model, in detailed and point-neuron versions.

Schmidt, M., Bakker, R., Shen, K., Bezgin, G., Diesmann, M. & van Albada, S. J. (2018). A multi-scale layer-resolved spiking network model of resting-state dynamics in macaque visual cortex. PLoS Computational Biology. — Many Potjans–Diesmann-like areas wired into a multi-area model.
Stimberg, M., Brette, R. & Goodman, D. F. M. (2019). Brian 2, an intuitive and efficient neural simulator. eLife. — Equation-based simulation; the fastest way to prototype a column.
Gewaltig, M.-O. & Diesmann, M. (2007). NEST (NEural Simulation Tool). Scholarpedia. — The large-scale point-neuron simulator behind the Potjans–Diesmann reference code.
Davison, A. P. et al. (2009). PyNN: a common interface for neuronal network simulators. Frontiers in Neuroinformatics. — Write once, run on NEST, NEURON, Brian or SpiNNaker.
Hines, M. L. & Carnevale, N. T. (1997). The NEURON simulation environment. Neural Computation. — The standard for multi-compartment models.
Bekolay, T. et al. (2014). Nengo: a Python tool for building large-scale functional brain models. Frontiers in Neuroinformatics. — Function-first spiking models via the Neural Engineering Framework.
Eshraghian, J. K. et al. (2023). Training spiking neural networks using lessons from deep learning. Proceedings of the IEEE. — The snnTorch tutorial-review; gradient-based SNN training.
Neftci, E. O., Mostafa, H. & Zenke, F. (2019). Surrogate gradient learning in spiking neural networks. IEEE Signal Processing Magazine. — Why and how surrogate gradients work.

Knight, J. C. & Nowotny, T. (2018). GPUs outperform current HPC and neuromorphic solutions in terms of speed and energy when simulating a highly-connected cortical model. Frontiers in Neuroscience. — GeNN on the Potjans–Diesmann model.

van Albada, S. J. et al. (2018). Performance comparison of the digital neuromorphic hardware SpiNNaker and the neural network simulation software NEST for a full-scale cortical microcircuit model. Frontiers in Neuroscience. — How to benchmark hardware honestly on a real cortical model.
Furber, S. B., Galluppi, F., Temple, S. & Plana, L. A. (2014). The SpiNNaker project. Proceedings of the IEEE. — Architecture of the ARM-based neuromorphic machine.
Davies, M. et al. (2018). Loihi: a neuromorphic manycore processor with on-chip learning. IEEE Micro. — Intel's chip with programmable on-chip plasticity.
Merolla, P. A. et al. (2014). A million spiking-neuron integrated circuit with a scalable communication network and interface. Science. — IBM TrueNorth.

Pehle, C. et al. (2022). The BrainScaleS-2 accelerated neuromorphic system with hybrid plasticity. Frontiers in Neuroscience. — Analog, faster-than-real-time neuromorphic computing with on-chip learning.

Start here: Gerstner, W., Kistler, W. M., Naud, R. & Paninski, L. (2014). Neuronal Dynamics: From Single Neurons to Networks and Models of Cognition. Cambridge University Press. — The best single book for spiking neurons, networks and plasticity; free online with an accompanying course.
Dayan, P. & Abbott, L. F. (2001). Theoretical Neuroscience. MIT Press. — The standard graduate textbook; rate models, coding and learning.
Eliasmith, C. & Anderson, C. H. (2003). Neural Engineering. MIT Press. — The Neural Engineering Framework behind Nengo.
Sherman, S. M. & Guillery, R. W. (2006). Exploring the Thalamus and Its Role in Cortical Function. MIT Press. — Thalamocortical loops in depth.
Braitenberg, V. & Schüz, A. (1998). Cortex: Statistics and Geometry of Neuronal Connectivity. Springer. — Quantitative anatomy of mouse cortex: synapse counts, densities, axon lengths.
Sterling, P. & Laughlin, S. (2015). Principles of Neural Design. MIT Press. — Energy and wiring constraints that shape neural codes; useful when designing for hardware.
Neuromatch Academy, Computational Neuroscience course (online, free). — Hands-on Python tutorials covering neuron models, dynamics and learning.
Thousand Brains Project and Numenta documentation (online). — Monty's code and documentation, plus Numenta's HTM resources, are the practical companion to the papers above.
